docs.title: Ceedling for VS Code
docs.text: This extension runs your Ceedling test suite from VS Code’s built-in Testing view. It lists every test file, test function, and parametrized case, and runs or debugs any of them from the view or the editor. It also reports failures at their lines, compiler problems in the editor, and code coverage in VS Code’s own coverage views.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
New to Ceedling?

Ceedling is a build system for C projects, built around unit tests with Unity and CMock. Ceedling’s own documentation explains how to set up a project, write tests, and configure builds.

Most VS Code Ceedling projects need no special configuration. Install the extension, open your Ceedling project’s folder, and the Testing view lists your tests.

Start Testing

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The site has four sections. The How-To guides start from what you want to do, and the User Manual from how each feature works.

  • How-To

    Step-by-step guides for common goals, from a first run to code coverage, debugging, and projects laid out your own way. Each ends with a complete, working example.

  • User Manual

    How each feature works, and every setting, from getting started to troubleshooting.

  • Releases

    What changed in each release, what’s known to be broken, and what to do when upgrading.

  • Help

    Reporting bugs, getting support and training, and supporting the project.

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
Help with the extension comes from its repository and from the Ceedling community. Bugs go to the extension’s issues, questions to the community forum, and support contracts and training to Ceedling Assist.

  • Report a Bug

    The extension’s GitHub issues. Check Troubleshooting and the Known Issues first, and include a debug-level log.

  • Ask the Community

    ThrowTheSwitch’s forum, for questions about Ceedling, Unity, CMock, and this extension. Ceedling’s documentation covers Ceedling itself.

  • Ceedling Assist

    Support contracts and training for Ceedling, from the people who make it.

  • Contribute

    How to build, test, and change the extension itself. Architecture.md explains how it works.

Supporting this work

Ceedling and its complementary ThrowTheSwitch pieces and parts are and always will be freely available and open source. Ceedling Suite is a growing collection of paid products and services built around Ceedling to help you do even more. Please consider supporting Ceedling and this extension as a GitHub Sponsor.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Four documents in the extension’s repository track its releases. The links below always show their current text. The version selector in this site’s header shows the documentation of other releases. Each minor release has one version, e.g. 2.1.0, which covers all its patch releases.

  • Changelog

    The terse, itemized record of what changed in each release. Read it to find when a feature or fix arrived.

  • Release Notes

    The narrative version, with each release’s highlights. Read it before upgrading.

  • Known Issues

    The open problems, by the Ceedling versions they affect. Read it before reporting a bug.

  • Breaking Changes

    What needs action when upgrading across a compatibility boundary. Read it when an upgrade changes behavior you rely on.

docs.title: How-To
docs.text:
The How-To guides walk through common goals step by step. Each one lists what it needs, and gives complete examples to paste. The User Manual explains every feature and setting they use.

  • Start Testing in Your Project

    Install the extension, open a project, and run its first test. Most projects need no configuration.

  • Debug a Test

    A launch configuration for Linux, macOS, or Windows, so any test runs under the debugger from its debug button.

  • Measure Code Coverage

    A coverage mixin with gcovr or ReportGenerator, so Run with Coverage shows each line’s hits.

  • See Compiler Errors in the Editor

    The gcc preset, or patterns of your own, so build errors appear at their lines and in the Problems panel.

  • Work With Several Projects

    Projects in subdirectories, several projects in one folder, multi-root workspaces, and project files of your own.

  • Run the Ceedling You Use

    Ceedling in a particular shell, through Bundler, vendored in the project, or selected by name.

  • Upgrade Ceedling

    A new Ceedling release, picked up with a refresh, and the old build layout cleaned out.

  • Write Parametrized Tests

    Unity’s TEST_CASE(), TEST_RANGE(), and TEST_MATRIX(), with each case listed and reported apart.

  • Find a Crashing Test

    Ceedling’s :use_backtrace, so a crash reports as a failure at the test that crashed.

  • Run Just One Test

    A single test function, run without the rest of its file, and what Ceedling still builds. A section of the User Manual.

docs.title: Run the Ceedling You Use
docs.text: This guide points the extension at the Ceedling a project actually uses: in a particular shell, through Bundler, or from another installation. The extension runs ceedling in each project’s directory, through the operating system’s default shell, so most installations need nothing. At the end, the extension’s commands run the same Ceedling a terminal does, at the version the project expects.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Ceedling that runs in a terminal. In the project’s directory, ceedling version should print the version you expect.

docs.title: Ceedling in a particular shell
docs.text:
Ceedling sometimes runs only in a shell of its own, as is common on Windows with MSYS2 or Git Bash. ceedlingExplorer.shellPath names that shell, and every Ceedling command runs in it.

MSYS2Git Bash 
{
    "ceedlingExplorer.shellPath": "C:/msys64/usr/bin/bash.exe"
}

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.shellPath": "C:/Program Files/Git/bin/bash.exe"
}

The shell must find Ceedling, and the compiler, on its own PATH. The extension runs each command as <shell> -c "<command>", which skips the login setup a terminal’s shell runs. MSYS2’s login setup adds its bin directories to PATH, for one. Check from a Windows terminal in the project’s directory, the way the extension runs it.

C:/msys64/usr/bin/bash.exe -c "ceedling version"

If that can’t find Ceedling, add the directories holding it and the compiler to the Windows PATH, e.g. C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin and C:\msys64\usr\bin.

docs.title: Ceedling through Bundler
docs.text:
A project that pins its Ceedling in a Gemfile runs it with bundle exec. ceedlingExplorer.ceedlingCommand holds the command that runs Ceedling.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.ceedlingCommand": "bundle exec ceedling"
}

The command runs in each project’s directory, so Bundler finds the Gemfile there or above it.

docs.title: A Ceedling vendored in the project
docs.text:
A project can carry its own copy of Ceedling in vendor/ceedling, as ceedling new --local makes. The installed ceedling, the launcher, then runs that copy for the project’s commands, and the extension needs no setting. The extension checks the copy’s version, and uses its features. A launcher before 1.2.2 can’t report another build’s release exactly, as the next section explains.

Replacing the copy, e.g. with ceedling upgrade ., changes its vendor/ceedling/lib/version.rb. The extension notices, and checks the project’s Ceedling again.

docs.title: Another installation, by name
docs.text:
Ceedling can run an installation other than the one ceedling starts, through the WHICH_CEEDLING environment variable or a project’s :project ↳ :which_ceedling setting. Either one names the installation’s directory, relative to the project’s directory, or gem for the installed gem. WHICH_CEEDLING outranks the setting, which outranks a vendor/ceedling copy.

:project:
  :which_ceedling: vendor/ceedling-1.2.2

The extension inherits VS Code’s own environment, so WHICH_CEEDLING must reach VS Code. Set it in the system’s environment, or in the shell that runs code. On macOS and Linux, VS Code also reads the login shell’s environment, so an export in a shell profile works too. Quit VS Code fully, and start it again, after changing the variable.

The launcher must be Ceedling 1.2.2 or later to report the other installation’s release exactly. Earlier launchers can’t tell, so the extension treats the project as the launcher’s own version. With WHICH_CEEDLING or a vendor/ceedling copy, its log warns about that. With :which_ceedling in the project file or a mixin, an earlier launcher never reads the setting, so no warning comes. Everything still works either way, though the Testing view waits for the project’s runs to finish before updating. Installing Ceedling 1.2.2 or later as the gem removes the wait.

docs.title: After changing installations
docs.text:
The extension checks each project’s Ceedling when it discovers the project. Some changes rediscover it by themselves, and one doesn’t.

  • A changed vendor/ceedling, project.yml, or mixin file rediscovers the folder’s projects.
  • A changed discovery setting, such as ceedlingExplorer.ceedlingCommand, rediscovers them too. Settings that only shape runs, such as ceedlingExplorer.testCommandArgs, take effect with the next run.
  • An upgraded gem needs a refresh. Choose the Testing view’s refresh button, so the extension checks the version again.

Upgrade Ceedling covers the rest of an upgrade.

docs.title: Measure Code Coverage
docs.text: This guide adds code coverage, so Run with Coverage shows which lines and branches your tests execute. It takes a report tool and a small mixin that enables Ceedling’s gcov plugin. At the end, the Test Coverage panel lists each source file’s coverage, and the editor marks each line’s hits.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A project the Testing view already lists. See Start Testing in Your Project.
  • GCC and its gcov. Ceedling’s gcov plugin builds its coverage tests with GCC, whatever compiler the project’s other tests use.
  • A report tool where Ceedling runs, either gcovr or ReportGenerator. gcovr is the usual choice. ReportGenerator, a .NET tool, is common on Windows.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install the report tool, in the shell Ceedling runs in.
  2. Save a coverage mixin as coverage.yml in the project’s directory, beside project.yml.
  3. Add the mixin to the folder’s .vscode/settings.json.
  4. Run with coverage. Choose Run with Coverage for a test, a file, or the whole project in the Testing view. The Test Coverage panel opens with the results.
gcovrReportGenerator

Install gcovr with Python’s pip.

pip install gcovr

The mixin enables the gcov plugin, with gcovr writing the Cobertura report the extension reads.

:plugins:
  :enabled:
    - gcov
:gcov:
  :utilities:
    - gcovr
  :reports:
    - Cobertura

Install ReportGenerator as a .NET global tool.

dotnet tool install -g dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool

The mixin enables the gcov plugin, with ReportGenerator writing the Cobertura report the extension reads.

:plugins:
  :enabled:
    - gcov
:gcov:
  :utilities:
    - ReportGenerator
  :reports:
    - Cobertura

The setting applies the mixin to every project in the folder that names no mixins of its own. A mixin’s path is relative to the project’s directory.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.mixins": ["coverage.yml"]
}

A mixin keeps the plugin out of project.yml, so builds outside VS Code stay as they were. Every run has the plugin available, and only coverage runs use it. The same settings can go in project.yml instead.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text: Each variation below changes one thing about the basic setup.

docs.title: Sources above the project
docs.text:
gcovr reports only sources beneath its report root, which is the project’s directory by default. A project whose sources sit above it, e.g. in a sibling ../src, needs a wider root. ReportGenerator includes every source directory in :paths: already.

:gcov:
  :gcovr:
    :report_root: ".."

docs.title: Coverage across several runs
docs.text:
Each coverage run shows only what it executed, since the extension clears earlier runs’ counters first. To add each run’s coverage to the last, as Ceedling itself does, turn the reset off.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.coverageResetsCounters": false
}

The counters then accumulate until ceedling clean or ceedling clobber. The Testing view’s Clean button clears them.

docs.title: Reports from a separate task
docs.text:
A project with :gcov: ↳ :report_task: set to TRUE writes reports only from Ceedling’s report:gcov task. The extension adds that task to each coverage run by itself, so no other setting is needed.

:gcov:
  :report_task: TRUE

docs.title: When no coverage appears
docs.text: A coverage run that shows nothing usually says why in a notification. The usual causes are a report tool missing from the shell’s PATH, or a report other than Cobertura. Code Coverage lists each reason and its fix.

docs.title: See Compiler Errors in the Editor
docs.text: This guide turns on problem matching, so compiler and linker errors appear in the editor and the Problems panel. The built-in gcc preset covers GCC, Clang, and the GNU linker, and takes one setting. Custom patterns cover the rest. At the end, a failed build marks each error and warning at its line, with the compiler’s message.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A project the Testing view already lists. See Start Testing in Your Project.

docs.title: Turn on the gcc preset
docs.text:
The gcc preset reads the warnings and errors GCC and Clang report, and the GNU linker’s “undefined reference” errors. Add it to the folder’s .vscode/settings.json.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.problemMatching": {
        "mode": "gcc"
    }
}

The next failed build’s errors and warnings then appear at their lines. Each build replaces the problems the last build of the same file or project reported, so a fixed error clears with the next build.

Ceedling shows a compiler’s output only when the compiler fails. A file that compiles with warnings and no errors therefore shows no problems, at Ceedling’s default verbosity. The macOS linker’s Undefined symbols errors don’t match the preset either, since they name no file and line.

docs.title: Add GCC’s notes
docs.text:
The preset leaves out GCC’s note: lines, which explain an error, e.g. the macro it came from. A custom pattern can report them at info severity.

Custom patterns replace the preset rather than adding to it, so a configuration that adds notes restates the preset first. Its first three patterns below are the preset’s own. The fourth reads notes.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.problemMatching": {
        "mode": "patterns",
        "patterns": [
            {
                "severity": "warning",
                "filePrefix": "${projectPath}",
                "regexp": "^(.*):(\\d+):(\\d+):\\s+warning:\\s+(.*)$",
                "message": 4, "file": 1, "line": 2, "column": 3
            },
            {
                "severity": "error",
                "filePrefix": "${projectPath}",
                "regexp": "^(.*):(\\d+):(\\d+):\\s+(?:fatal\\s+)?error:\\s+(.*)$",
                "message": 4, "file": 1, "line": 2, "column": 3
            },
            {
                "severity": "error",
                "regexp": "^(.*):(\\d+):(?:\\([^)]*\\):)?\\s+(?!(warning:|error:|note:|fatal error:))(.*)$",
                "message": 4, "file": 1, "line": 2
            },
            {
                "severity": "info",
                "filePrefix": "${projectPath}",
                "regexp": "^(.*):(\\d+):(\\d+):\\s+note:\\s+(.*)$",
                "message": 4, "file": 1, "line": 2, "column": 3
            }
        ]
    }
}

Each pattern reads one kind of line.

  • Warnings and errors read GCC’s file:line:column: warning: message form. Group 1 is the file, 2 the line, 3 the column, and 4 the message. filePrefix makes the relative file absolute, from the project’s directory.
  • Linker errors read the GNU linker’s file:line:(.text+0x18): undefined reference to 'f' form, with or without the section in parentheses. The linker reports an absolute file, so this pattern needs no filePrefix. Its message is group 4. Group 3 sits inside the lookahead that skips the other forms, and never matches.
  • Notes read the same form as warnings, with note:.

docs.title: Another compiler
docs.text:
A compiler with its own message format needs a pattern of its own. IAR’s compilers, for example, report "file",line Severity[tag]: message. These two patterns read its warnings and errors.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.problemMatching": {
        "mode": "patterns",
        "patterns": [
            {
                "severity": "warning",
                "filePrefix": "${projectPath}",
                "regexp": "^\"(.*)\",(\\d+)\\s+Warning\\[\\w+\\]:\\s+(.*)$",
                "message": 3, "file": 1, "line": 2
            },
            {
                "severity": "error",
                "filePrefix": "${projectPath}",
                "regexp": "^\"(.*)\",(\\d+)\\s+(?:Fatal )?[Ee]rror\\[\\w+\\]:\\s+(.*)$",
                "message": 3, "file": 1, "line": 2
            }
        ]
    }
}

docs.title: Write your own
docs.text:
A pattern is a regular expression for one line of the compiler’s output, plus the numbers of its capture groups. Start from a real line, taken from the Test Results panel after a failed build.

  1. Copy a problem line from the Test Results panel.
  2. Write a regular expression that matches it, with a group each for the file, the line, and the message. regex101 helps, with its ECMAScript flavor.
  3. Double each backslash for JSON, so \d becomes \\d.
  4. Number the groups in file, line, and message, plus column if the line has one.
  5. Set filePrefix to ${projectPath} if the compiler reports files relative to the project.

Ceedling reports a failed tool’s output on its own stderr, which patterns scan by default. A pattern for something Ceedling writes to stdout needs "scanStdout": true. Problem Matching lists every pattern property.

docs.title: Find a Crashing Test
docs.text: This guide finds the test that crashed, without starting a debugger. Ceedling’s own :use_backtrace setting does the work, and its default already reports which test case crashed. With gdb, it also finds the crashing line. At the end, a crash shows as a failed test in the Testing view, at the test that crashed.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A project the Testing view already lists. See Start Testing in Your Project.
  • For the :gdb choice, gdb installed where Ceedling runs, and tests built for the native platform.

docs.title: Choose how to find the crash
docs.text:
A crash stops a test executable before it reports, so Ceedling reruns the file’s tests to find which one crashed. The setting chooses how, at different costs.

Choice Finds Needs Suits :simple, the default The test case that crashed Nothing more Every test fixture, simulators and cross builds included :gdb The test case and the crashing line gdb, and a native build Tests that run on the build machine itself :none Nothing. Every test in the file fails as crashed Nothing Builds where reruns cost too much

:simple reruns each test case of the crashed file on its own. :gdb reruns each one under gdb, which reports where the crash happened.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Choose a setting, from the table above. A project that sets none gets :simple.
  2. Add it to project.yml, or to a mixin.
  3. Run the tests. A crashing test shows as failed, with Ceedling’s account of the crash as its message.
simplegdb 
:project:
  :use_backtrace: :simple

:project:
  :use_backtrace: :gdb

docs.title: What a crash looks like
docs.text:
A crashed test fails like any other, in the Testing view and in the editor. With :gdb, its message tells where the test crashed, and its failure sits at the line gdb reports.

On Ceedling 1.1.0 and later, :gdb also writes a gdb log for each test case. The failure message’s reference to that log is a link. Choose it to open the log, with gdb’s full backtrace.

docs.title: When you need the debugger
docs.text: A crash found this way often still needs a closer look. Debug a Test runs the test file under the debugger, stopping at your breakpoints.

docs.title: Debug a Test
docs.text: This guide sets up debugging, so any test runs under the debugger from its debug button. It takes a debugger extension and one launch.json configuration. At the end, a test’s debug button builds its file and stops at your breakpoints.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A project the Testing view already lists. See Start Testing in Your Project.
  • A native debugger: gdb on Linux and Windows, lldb on macOS.
  • A VS Code debugger extension. Microsoft’s C/C++ extension, ms-vscode.cpptools, drives gdb and lldb. On macOS, CodeLLDB, vadimcn.vscode-lldb, brings its own lldb.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install the debugger extension, from VS Code’s Extensions view.
  2. Add a launch configuration. Open .vscode/launch.json in the workspace folder, creating it if needed, and add the configuration for your platform below. Name it ceedling, which the extension looks for by default.
  3. Set a breakpoint in a test function.
  4. Debug the test. Choose the debug button beside the test, in the Testing view or the editor’s gutter. The extension builds and runs the test file, then starts the debugger at your breakpoint.

docs.title: A configuration for each platform
docs.text:
Each configuration names the test executable with the token ${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}. The extension replaces it with the executable’s path, relative to the test/out/ directory under the project’s build root. The examples assume the build root is build, as ceedling new sets it.

LinuxmacOSWindows

The C/C++ extension with gdb.

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "ceedling",
            "type": "cppdbg",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/build/test/out/${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}",
            "args": [],
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}",
            "MIMode": "gdb",
            "setupCommands": [
                { "description": "Enable pretty-printing for gdb", "text": "-enable-pretty-printing", "ignoreFailures": true }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

CodeLLDB, which bundles its own lldb and needs nothing else installed.

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "ceedling",
            "type": "lldb",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/build/test/out/${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}",
            "args": [],
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}"
        }
    ]
}

The C/C++ extension drives lldb too, with "MIMode": "lldb".

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "ceedling",
            "type": "cppdbg",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/build/test/out/${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}",
            "args": [],
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}",
            "MIMode": "lldb"
        }
    ]
}

The C/C++ extension with the gdb of MinGW or MSYS2. miDebuggerPath names it. This one is MSYS2’s UCRT64 gdb.

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "ceedling",
            "type": "cppdbg",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/build/test/out/${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}",
            "args": [],
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}",
            "MIMode": "gdb",
            "miDebuggerPath": "C:/msys64/ucrt64/bin/gdb.exe",
            "setupCommands": [
                { "description": "Enable pretty-printing for gdb", "text": "-enable-pretty-printing", "ignoreFailures": true }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

The debugger must match the compiler that built the tests, e.g. MSYS2 UCRT64’s gdb for its gcc.

docs.title: Several projects
docs.text:
Each project in ceedlingExplorer.projects names its own configuration in debugLaunchConfig. Projects in subdirectories need configurations whose program includes the subdirectory.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.projects": [
        { "path": "app", "debugLaunchConfig": "Debug app test" },
        { "path": "bootloader", "debugLaunchConfig": "Debug bootloader test" }
    ]
}

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "Debug app test",
            "type": "cppdbg",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/app/build/test/out/${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}",
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}/app",
            "MIMode": "gdb"
        },
        {
            "name": "Debug bootloader test",
            "type": "cppdbg",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/bootloader/build/test/out/${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}",
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}/bootloader",
            "MIMode": "gdb"
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: A build root of your own
docs.text:
A project that moves its build with :project ↳ :build_root moves the executable with it. The program path then starts with that build root instead of build.

:project:
  :build_root: out

With that build root, program becomes ${workspaceFolder}/out/test/out/${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
A debug session covers a whole test file, since Ceedling builds each file into one executable. The file’s other tests run too, so set breakpoints in the test you care about.

Start a session only from a test’s debug button. Starting the configuration with F5 shows an error, since only a test’s debug button tells the extension which executable to debug. Debugging explains the whole sequence.

docs.title: Start Testing in Your Project
docs.text: This guide takes a typical Ceedling project from opening it in VS Code to running its first test. Most projects need no configuration, so it usually takes a minute. At the end, the Testing view lists every test, and runs any of them.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• VS Code 1.88.0 or later.
  • Ceedling 1.0.0 or later, which runs in a terminal. ceedling version should print its version.
  • A Ceedling project, with its project.yml, or ceedling.yml from Ceedling 1.2.0.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install the extension. Search VS Code’s Extensions view for “Ceedling”, and install Ceedling by Throw The Switch.
  2. Open the project. Open the folder holding the project file, with File ↳ Open Folder….
  3. Open the Testing view. Choose the flask icon in the Activity Bar. After a few seconds, the view lists the project’s test files, each with its test functions.
  4. Run a test. Choose the run button beside a test function. Its result appears beside it, and a failure shows its message at the failing line in the editor.
  5. Run them all. Choose Run Tests at the top of the view, to run every test file.

The editor’s gutter shows run and debug buttons beside each test function too.

docs.title: When no tests appear
docs.text:
The extension looks for the project file at the folder’s root. Two settings cover most projects where it isn’t found, or where Ceedling won’t run.

A project in a subdirectory needs its path in ceedlingExplorer.projects. Add it to the folder’s .vscode/settings.json.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.projects": [
        { "path": "firmware" }
    ]
}

A Ceedling that runs only in a particular shell needs that shell in ceedlingExplorer.shellPath. That is common on Windows, where Ceedling may run only in an MSYS2 or Git Bash shell. Run the Ceedling You Use shows each setup.

Any other problem shows a notification. Troubleshooting matches each message to its fix.

docs.title: What happens when the folder opens
docs.text:
The extension asks Ceedling itself about the project, so it sees exactly what a real build sees. It runs ceedling version, then ceedling dumpconfig and ceedling files:test, in the project’s directory. It then reads each test file for its test functions. Getting Started explains each step.

The test list keeps itself current from then on. Editing a test file updates its tests as you type. Adding a test file, or changing project.yml, rediscovers the project.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Debug a Test adds a launch configuration, so any test runs under the debugger.
  • Measure Code Coverage adds Ceedling’s gcov plugin, for Run with Coverage.
  • See Compiler Errors in the Editor puts compiler and linker errors in the Problems panel.

docs.title: Write Parametrized Tests
docs.text: This guide sets up Unity’s parametrized tests, which run one test function once per set of arguments. It takes one project setting, and one marker line above each function. At the end, the Testing view lists each case beneath its function, with its own result.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A project the Testing view already lists. See Start Testing in Your Project.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Enable parametrized tests. Add the setting below to project.yml, or to a mixin.
  2. On Ceedling 1.0.0, turn test preprocessing off. Its preprocessing loses the markers. Set :project ↳ :use_test_preprocessor to :none, its default, or to :mocks. Ceedling 1.1.0 and later handle the markers either way.
  3. Mark a test function with TEST_CASE(), TEST_RANGE(), or TEST_MATRIX(), and give it parameters.
  4. Run it. Each case appears beneath its function, labeled with its arguments.
:unity:
  :use_param_tests: true

docs.title: The three markers
docs.text:
Each marker produces cases in its own way, and a function may carry several.

TEST_CASE() lists one case’s arguments. Repeat it for each case.

TEST_CASE(1, 2, 3)
TEST_CASE(-1, 1, 0)
void test_AddReturnsTheSum(int a, int b, int sum)
{
    TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL(sum, add(a, b));
}

The Testing view lists two cases, 1, 2, 3 and -1, 1, 0.

TEST_RANGE() steps each parameter through a range, [start, end, step]. Square brackets include the end, and angle brackets, <start, end, step>, exclude it. With several ranges, the cases are every combination.

TEST_RANGE([0, 2, 1])
void test_LedIndexIsValid(int index)
{
    TEST_ASSERT_TRUE(led_is_valid(index));
}

The view lists three cases, 0, 1, and 2.

TEST_MATRIX() lists each parameter’s values, and the cases are every combination.

TEST_MATRIX([1, 2], [3, 4])
void test_ProductIsPositive(int a, int b)
{
    TEST_ASSERT_TRUE(a * b > 0);
}

The view lists four cases, 1, 3, 1, 4, 2, 3, and 2, 4.

docs.title: Running cases
docs.text: A case runs with all the other cases of its function, since Ceedling selects tests by function. Every case still reports its own result, and a failed case shows its message at its marker. Debugging a case debugs its whole test file. Running Tests explains both.

docs.title: Upgrade Ceedling
docs.text: This guide upgrades a project’s Ceedling and brings the extension along. The extension follows each Ceedling version’s features by itself, so an upgrade mostly takes a refresh. An upgrade to Ceedling 1.2.2 also needs one clobber, to remove the old build layout. At the end, the Testing view runs the new Ceedling, with no output left from the old one.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • The Ceedling release to upgrade to, 1.0.0 or later. Ceedling 1.0.0 through 1.2.2 are supported.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Upgrade Ceedling. Install the new gem, e.g. with gem install ceedling. For a project that vendors its Ceedling in vendor/ceedling, also run ceedling upgrade . in the project’s directory, which copies the installed Ceedling into it.
  2. Refresh the Testing view with its refresh button, after a gem upgrade. The extension checks the version again. A changed vendor/ceedling refreshes by itself.
  3. Run the tests, to build them with the new Ceedling.
  4. Clobber, when upgrading to 1.2.2 or later from an earlier release. See below.

docs.title: Upgrading to Ceedling 1.2.2
docs.text:
Ceedling 1.2.2 builds each test in a new place, under its path from the project’s root. An earlier release’s build output stays where it was until a clobber removes it. Coverage reports still read that output’s counters, so it can skew coverage.

How the old output goes depends on the release you upgrade from.

  • From 1.2.0 or 1.2.1, the first build warns about the old layout, and the extension offers to clobber the project. Choose Clobber. The clobber waits for the runs under way to finish.
  • From an earlier release, no warning comes. Clobber once with the Testing view’s Clobber button.

Until the clobber, with ceedlingExplorer.coverageResetsCounters on, its default, coverage stays exact, since each coverage run clears the counters first. With it off, coverage counts the old layout’s counters too, until the clobber.

docs.title: Launch configurations
docs.text: Launch configurations need no change. The debug token’s path follows each Ceedling version’s own build layout, under the same build/test/out/ directory. See Debugging.

docs.title: When something breaks
docs.text: The Breaking Changes describe the changes that need action when upgrading, and the Known Issues list the open problems by Ceedling version. Troubleshooting matches each notification to its fix.

docs.title: Work With Several Projects
docs.text: This guide sets up workspaces that hold Ceedling projects somewhere other than the folder’s root, or more than one of them. Each layout below takes one setting, ceedlingExplorer.projects, in the folder’s .vscode/settings.json. At the end, the Testing view lists each project, and runs, debugs, and measures each one with its own configuration.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • Ceedling projects the extension can run. See Start Testing in Your Project.

docs.title: A project in a subdirectory
docs.text:
A project file outside the folder’s root needs the project’s directory in path. Paths are relative to the workspace folder.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.projects": [
        { "path": "firmware" }
    ]
}

docs.title: Several projects in one folder
docs.text:
A folder holding several projects lists each one. The Testing view then shows each project by its name, with its test files beneath it. Each project can name its own launch configuration and mixins.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.mixins": ["mixins/common.yml"],
    "ceedlingExplorer.projects": [
        { "path": "app", "name": "Application", "debugLaunchConfig": "Debug app test" },
        { "path": "bootloader", "name": "Bootloader", "mixins": ["gcc", "mixins/bootloader.yml"] },
        { "path": "tools/codec", "name": "Codec", "mixins": [] }
    ]
}

The three projects take their mixins three ways.

  • Application names no mixins, so it takes ceedlingExplorer.mixins. The mixin’s path is relative to the project’s own directory, so it is app/mixins/common.yml.
  • Bootloader names its own, which replace the folder’s list. gcc is one of Ceedling’s built-in toolchain targets, from Ceedling 1.1.0, named without a path.
  • Codec names an empty list, so it takes no mixins at all.

docs.title: Several workspace folders
docs.text:
A multi-root workspace lists each folder’s projects under an entry of its own, labeled Ceedling (folder). Each folder reads its own .vscode/settings.json, so each can describe its projects differently.

{
    "folders": [
        { "path": "product" },
        { "path": "shared-libraries" }
    ]
}

The .code-workspace file above lists the folders. Each folder’s own settings file then names its projects, e.g. shared-libraries/.vscode/settings.json.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.projects": [
        { "path": "ring-buffer" },
        { "path": "crc" }
    ]
}

A folder without a Ceedling project adds no entry.

docs.title: A project file of your own
docs.text:
A path can name a YAML file instead of a directory. A file named project.yml is the project itself. Any other file is applied as a mixin over the project.yml beside it. That suits a variant of a project, e.g. one for CI or a simulator, kept beside the main file.

{
    "ceedlingExplorer.projects": [
        { "path": "firmware/project.yml", "name": "Firmware" },
        { "path": "firmware/simulator.yml", "name": "Firmware on the simulator" }
    ]
}

From Ceedling 1.2.0, a directory may hold ceedling.yml in place of project.yml. The extension finds either one. A directory holding both is an error, as Ceedling itself reports it. Name the one to use in path to settle it.

docs.title: Same-named test files
docs.text:
Two test files may share a name in different directories, e.g. test/unit/test_buffer.c and test/integration/test_buffer.c. What works depends on the Ceedling version.

Ceedling Runs and results Debugging Coverage 1.2.2 and later Each file apart Each file apart Each file apart 1.2.1 Each file apart, with one exception Each file apart, with one exception Each file apart, with one exception 1.2.0 Each file apart, with one exception Each file apart, with one exception Fails with an ambiguous file reference Before 1.2.0 May run the other file May debug the other file May run the other file

Ceedling 1.2.0 and later tell the files apart by their paths, and so does the extension. Before that, Ceedling names a test file by its name alone. The extension’s log warns when a coverage run can’t tell the files apart.

Ceedling 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 make one exception. They can’t build a test file whose path within the test path ends another same-named file’s path, e.g. test/test_calc.c beside test/unit/test_calc.c. Ceedling 1.2.2 builds both. The Known Issues describe it.

docs.title: User Manual
docs.text:
The User Manual explains how each of the extension’s features works, and lists every setting. Read a page to understand a feature, or to look up an option. The How-To guides instead walk through common goals step by step.

  • Getting Started

    What the extension requires, and how to install it. How it reads a project, and keeps its test list current.

  • Running Tests

    What each kind of run does in Ceedling, from a whole workspace to a single test. How results and labels appear, and the Clean and Clobber commands.

  • Debugging

    How a debug session builds a test file and starts your debugger. The launch configuration and its token, and what a session covers.

  • Code Coverage

    How coverage runs work with Ceedling’s gcov plugin. What gcovr and ReportGenerator each report, and why a run might show none.

  • Problem Matching

    How compiler and linker problems reach the editor and the Problems panel. The setting’s fields and every pattern property.

  • Configuration

    Every setting, with its default. Mixins, and the extension’s commands.

  • Troubleshooting

    Each common symptom and message, with its cause and fix. Reading the extension’s log, and reporting a bug.

docs.title: Code Coverage
docs.text: Run with Coverage runs tests through Ceedling’s gcov plugin and shows what they executed in VS Code’s coverage views. This page covers how coverage runs work, what each report tool includes, and why a run might show none. The coverage guide sets it up step by step, with gcovr or ReportGenerator.

docs.title: What a coverage run shows
docs.text:
A coverage run shows each source file’s line, branch, and function coverage. The Test Coverage panel lists every file the report covers. In the editor, inline coverage marks each line’s hit count and each branch’s outcome. Test results appear in the Testing view exactly as for a plain run.

The Testing view offers Run with Coverage, beside Run and Debug, while a project enables the gcov plugin. A coverage run rebuilds the tests with coverage instrumentation, which is slower. Plain runs don’t pay that cost, since only coverage runs use the plugin.

docs.title: What coverage needs
docs.text:
Coverage needs three pieces where Ceedling runs.

  • Ceedling’s gcov plugin, enabled in project.yml or a mixin.
  • gcov, from the GCC toolchain.
  • A report tool, either gcovr or ReportGenerator. Install gcovr with pip install gcovr. Install ReportGenerator, a .NET tool common on Windows, with dotnet tool install -g dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool.

The extension reads the Cobertura XML report either tool writes, so the project must list Cobertura among :gcov: ↳ :reports:.

:plugins:
  :enabled:
    - gcov
:gcov:
  :utilities:
    - gcovr           # or ReportGenerator, or both
  :reports:
    - Cobertura       # the report the extension reads; add any others you want

A mixin keeps these settings out of project.yml. Save the YAML above as, e.g., coverage.yml, and add it to ceedlingExplorer.mixins. Every run then has the plugin available, and only coverage runs use it.

docs.title: How coverage runs work
docs.text:
A coverage run uses Ceedling’s gcov: tasks in place of test: tasks. The ceedlingExplorer.coverageCommandArgs setting holds the task, as ceedlingExplorer.testCommandArgs holds a plain run’s.

  • One run, one measurement. Each coverage run shows only what it executed. The tools report every coverage counter in the build directory, so the extension clears the counters earlier runs left before each coverage run. To accumulate coverage across runs instead, as Ceedling itself does until ceedling clean or clobber, set ceedlingExplorer.coverageResetsCounters to false.
  • Overlapping runs. Two coverage runs at once in the same build directory share its counters, so each may show some of the other’s coverage.
  • Which report. With both tools enabled, the extension reads gcovr’s report.
  • Deferred reports. With :gcov: ↳ :report_task: TRUE, reports come only from Ceedling’s report:gcov task. A coverage run then adds that task to its own command line.
  • Several projects. A run spanning several projects shows their coverage together. A source file that several projects test shows their combined hits.
  • Projects without the plugin. A coverage run still runs their tests, and a notification says why they have no coverage.
  • Same-named test files. Before Ceedling 1.2.1, gcov: tasks take a test file’s name without its directory, so they can’t tell apart same-named test files in different directories. Ceedling 1.2.0 then stops with an ambiguous file reference error, and earlier versions may run the other file. The extension warns in its log when that applies. Ceedling 1.2.1 and later take the file’s path, as test: tasks do.

docs.title: What each tool reports
docs.text:
gcovr and ReportGenerator write the same report format, but they differ in what they include.

  • Sources outside the project. gcovr reports only files beneath its :gcov: ↳ :gcovr: ↳ :report_root:, which defaults to the project directory. To include sources above the project, set it to a directory that holds them all, e.g. "..". ReportGenerator includes every source directory in :paths:.
  • Functions. The Test Coverage panel lists functions when the report names them. ReportGenerator’s reports do. gcovr’s do in some versions, e.g. 8.6, and not in others, e.g. 5.0 and 7.2. Line and branch coverage appear either way.
  • Sources earlier runs built. ReportGenerator lists every source an earlier coverage build compiled, at 0% when this run didn’t execute it. gcovr leaves those out.

docs.title: When no coverage appears
docs.text:
A run can show no coverage for a handful of reasons, and a notification names most of them. Each reason is notified once a session. Every run also logs it, and notes it in the Test Results panel beside Ceedling’s full output.

  • No Cobertura report configured. A notification says to add Cobertura to :gcov: ↳ :reports:.
  • No report tool. The report tool isn’t installed where Ceedling runs, or isn’t on that shell’s PATH. A notification names the report it expected.
  • No sources in the report. A notification says so. gcovr reports only sources beneath its :report_root:, as above.
  • A failed build. No report is written, and the Testing view shows the build’s errors.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: This page is the reference for every setting and command the extension contributes. Most projects need none of them. The How-To guides show the settings at work in complete examples.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The extension’s settings live under ceedlingExplorer in VS Code’s settings. Set them in a workspace’s or a folder’s .vscode/settings.json to suit one project, or in your user settings to suit them all. VS Code’s Settings editor lists them too, under Extensions ↳ Ceedling project configuration.

Each setting below gives its default. A setting left unset takes its default.

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.projects
docs.text:
Default: []

The Ceedling projects in the workspace folder, one entry each. With none, the folder itself is the project, with its project.yml at the folder’s root. From Ceedling 1.2.0, ceedling.yml works there too.

"ceedlingExplorer.projects": [
    {
        "path": "firmware",
        "name": "Firmware",
        "debugLaunchConfig": "Debug firmware test"
    }
]

Each entry has four fields.

  • path names the project, relative to the workspace folder. It is required. It is either a directory holding a project.yml, or a YAML file, .yml or .yaml. A YAML file other than project.yml is applied as a mixin over the project.yml beside it. With Ceedling 1.2.0 and later, ceedling.yml works in place of project.yml, but a directory may not hold both.
  • name labels the project in the Testing view, which lists projects by name when a folder holds several. Without it, the label is the path. A YAML file other than project.yml gives its file name, without the extension. Each label must be unique, since a later entry with the same one replaces the earlier.
  • debugLaunchConfig is the name of the launch.json configuration that debugs the project’s tests. Without it, the project debugs with a configuration named ceedling. See Debugging.
  • mixins are the project’s own mixins, lowest to highest priority. Without them, the project uses ceedlingExplorer.mixins. An explicit [] opts the project out of that workspace-wide list.

Without any entry, the extension also expects a debug configuration named ceedling.

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.mixins
docs.text:
Default: []

The mixins applied to every project that doesn’t name its own, lowest to highest priority. Each entry is one of three things. A name, without a path or extension, is a mixin Ceedling finds through its mixin load paths. Ceedling’s built-in toolchain targets, such as gcc or clang, are named this way. A path names a YAML file, relative to the project’s directory.

"ceedlingExplorer.mixins": ["gcc", "mixins/coverage.yml"]

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.shellPath
docs.text:
Default: null

The path to the shell Ceedling runs in. With null, Ceedling runs in the operating system’s default shell. Set it when Ceedling runs only in a particular shell, as is common on Windows with MSYS2 or Git Bash.

"ceedlingExplorer.shellPath": "C:/msys64/usr/bin/bash.exe"

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.ceedlingCommand
docs.text:
Default: "ceedling"

The command that runs Ceedling. Set it to run Ceedling through Bundler, or from a path of its own.

"ceedlingExplorer.ceedlingCommand": "bundle exec ceedling"

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.testCommandArgs
docs.text:
Default: ["test:${TEST_ID}"]

The arguments that run one test file. Their ${TEST_ID} tag becomes the test file, or all when a run covers a whole project. With Ceedling 1.2.0 and later, the test file is its project-relative path, e.g. test/unit/test_foo.c, which tells same-named test files apart. With earlier versions, it is the file’s name alone. Coverage runs use ceedlingExplorer.coverageCommandArgs instead.

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.coverageCommandArgs
docs.text:
Default: ["gcov:${TEST_ID}"]

The arguments that run one test file with coverage. Their ${TEST_ID} tag becomes the test file, or all when a run covers a whole project. With Ceedling 1.2.1 and later, the test file is its project-relative path, as for testCommandArgs. With earlier versions, it is the file’s name alone, as their gcov: tasks require.

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.coverageResetsCounters
docs.text:
Default: true

Whether each coverage run first clears the coverage counters earlier runs left, so it shows only what it executed. Set it to false to accumulate coverage across runs instead, as Ceedling itself does until a clean or clobber.

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.prettyTestLabel
docs.text:
Default: true

Shortens each test’s label in the Testing view by dropping its prefix. For example, test_BlinkTaskShouldToggleLed becomes BlinkTaskShouldToggleLed. Running Tests shows both forms.

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.prettyTestFileLabel
docs.text:
Default: true

Shortens each test file’s label by dropping its path, prefix, and extension. For example, test/LEDs/test_BlinkTask.c becomes BlinkTask. Running Tests shows both forms.

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.problemMatching
docs.text:
Default: none. Its mode field defaults to "disabled", and its patterns field to [].

Reports compiler and linker problems in the editor and the Problems panel. Problem matching is off until mode selects a preset or custom patterns.

"ceedlingExplorer.problemMatching": {
    "mode": "gcc"
}

Problem Matching explains both fields and every pattern property.

docs.title: ceedlingExplorer.ansiEscapeSequencesRemoved
docs.text:
Default: true

Whether ANSI escape sequences, such as terminal colors, are removed from Ceedling’s output before the extension reads it and shows it.

docs.title: Mixins
docs.text:
A Ceedling mixin is a YAML fragment merged into a project’s configuration at build time. Mixins suit toolchain targets, CI overrides, and configuration that shouldn’t be copied into every project.yml.

Two settings configure them. ceedlingExplorer.mixins applies to every project, and ceedlingExplorer.projects[].mixins replaces it for one project. Later entries win on conflicts, matching the precedence of Ceedling’s own --mixin option. The extension passes them to the Ceedling commands it runs for a project, from the ceedling dumpconfig that reads its configuration to each test run.

The extension always applies one more mixin, after any you configure. It enables the report_tests_log_factory plugin’s cppunit report, which is where the Testing view reads results. This mixin always takes the highest priority, so no project file or mixin can turn the report off. Only an invalid mixin keeps it from applying, and discovery then stops with an error. Enabling report_tests_log_factory yourself as well is harmless.

The extension warns once if the CppUnit report has a name other than its default. That happens when project.yml or a mixin sets :report_tests_log_factory ↳ :cppunit ↳ :filename. The extension still finds the report. The warning only points out the unusual name, in case it wasn’t intended.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Two commands run Ceedling’s cleanup tasks in every Ceedling project in the workspace. They appear in the Command Palette and as buttons in the Testing view’s toolbar. Each project’s command waits for any Ceedling build under way in that project to finish.

ID Command Runs ceedlingExplorer.clean Ceedling: Clean ceedling clean ceedlingExplorer.clobber Ceedling: Clobber ceedling clobber

Bind a keyboard shortcut to either by its ID. Running, debugging, and refreshing tests use VS Code’s own Testing commands.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Debugging a test builds its test file, runs it, then starts your debugger on the test executable Ceedling built. The extension supplies the executable’s path to a launch.json configuration you provide. This page covers how that works, what a session covers, and how crashing tests are caught without a debugger. Debug a Test has ready-to-use configurations for Linux, macOS, and Windows.

docs.title: The launch configuration
docs.text:
Each project debugs with the launch.json configuration that its ceedlingExplorer.projects entry names in debugLaunchConfig. The setting holds the configuration’s name, its "name" field. A project that names none, like a folder without any ceedlingExplorer.projects entry, debugs with a configuration named ceedling.

The configuration’s program names the test executable with ${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}. The extension replaces this token with the executable’s path, relative to the project’s test output directory. That directory is test/out/ under the project’s :project ↳ :build_root, so build/test/out/ in a project ceedling new made. So program starts with the project’s own path to it.

This example uses Microsoft’s C/C++ extension, ms-vscode.cpptools, with gdb.

{
    "name": "ceedling",
    "type": "cppdbg",
    "request": "launch",
    "program": "${workspaceFolder}/build/test/out/${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable}",
    "args": [],
    "stopAtEntry": false,
    "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}",
    "environment": [],
    "externalConsole": false,
    "MIMode": "gdb",
    "setupCommands": [
        {
            "description": "Enable pretty-printing for gdb",
            "text": "-enable-pretty-printing",
            "ignoreFailures": true
        }
    ]
}

On Windows, add "miDebuggerPath" with the path to MinGW’s or MSYS2’s gdb.exe, e.g. "C:/msys64/ucrt64/bin/gdb.exe".

A project in a subdirectory of the workspace folder includes that directory, e.g. ${workspaceFolder}/firmware/build/test/out/. The token’s part of the path follows the Ceedling version’s own build layout, so the same configuration works across Ceedling upgrades.

docs.title: Starting a debug session
docs.text:
Debugging must start from a test’s debug button, in the Testing view or the editor’s gutter. The extension replaces the token only then. Starting the same configuration with F5, or from the Run and Debug view, leaves the token unresolved. A clear error then says to start from a test’s debug button, instead of a confusing “path does not exist” failure.

A debug session takes three steps.

  1. The extension builds and runs the test file, as a plain run does. The Testing view shows that run’s real results.
  2. It finds the executable that build just wrote, and replaces the token with its path.
  3. It starts the configuration. The session ends when the debugger stops, or when you cancel the run.

A failed build starts no debugger. The Testing view and the Test Results panel show the build’s errors.

docs.title: What a session covers
docs.text:
Debugging always covers a whole test file. Ceedling compiles and runs each test file as one executable, so debugging one test function, or one parametrized case, still debugs its entire file. Set breakpoints in the test you care about, and expect the file’s other tests to run too.

Debugging several files at once debugs only the first, with a notification saying so.

docs.title: Crashing tests
docs.text:
Finding a crashing test needs no debugger. Ceedling’s own :use_backtrace project setting reports a crash as a failed test, at the test case that crashed. The extension shows that failure like any other, with no extra configuration.

The setting offers three choices.

  • :simple, the default, reruns each test case of the crashed file on its own, to find which one crashed. It needs no gdb. It also works with a simulator-based test fixture, not just native builds.
  • :none reruns nothing, and reports every test in the crashed file as failed.
  • :gdb also finds the exact crashing line. On Ceedling 1.1.0 and later, it writes a gdb log file per test case, and the extension turns the failure message’s reference to that log into a clickable link. :gdb needs gdb installed, and supports only the native build platform. Stay on :simple for a cross-compiled or simulator-based test fixture.
:project:
  :use_backtrace: :gdb

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: The extension brings a Ceedling project’s tests into VS Code’s built-in Testing view, and most projects need no configuration at all. This page covers what the extension requires, how to install it, and what it does when it opens a project. The first-run guide walks through the same steps for a typical project.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The extension needs a recent VS Code and Ceedling 1.0.0 or later.

  • VS Code 1.88.0 or later. That release added the test coverage views that Run with Coverage uses.
  • Ceedling 1.0.0 or later. Ceedling 1.0.0 through 1.2.2 are supported. The Ceedling documentation covers installing it.
  • Code coverage also needs Ceedling’s gcov plugin and a coverage report tool. See Code Coverage.
  • Debugging needs a debugger extension, such as Microsoft’s C/C++ extension, and a launch.json configuration. See Debugging.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text: Install the extension from the Visual Studio Marketplace. Search the Extensions view for “Ceedling”, or open the Marketplace page. Its identifier is throw-the-switch.vscode-ceedling.

docs.title: Opening a project
docs.text:
Open the folder or workspace containing your Ceedling project, then open the Testing view, the flask icon in the Activity Bar. The view lists every test file, test function, and parametrized test case. Run and debug tests from it, or from the icons beside each test in the editor.

Two settings cover most projects that don’t work straight away.

  • When the project file isn’t at the folder’s root, name the project in ceedlingExplorer.projects.
  • When Ceedling runs only in a particular shell, as is common on Windows, set ceedlingExplorer.shellPath.

A workspace with several folders lists each folder’s projects under an entry of its own, labeled Ceedling (folder). A folder without a Ceedling project adds no entry.

docs.title: How the extension reads a project
docs.text:
The extension asks Ceedling itself for each project’s configuration, so it sees exactly what a real build sees. Discovering a project takes three Ceedling commands, run in the project’s directory.

  1. ceedling version checks that Ceedling runs and is 1.0.0 or later. It honors a Ceedling vendored in the project’s vendor/ceedling, or named by WHICH_CEEDLING. From Ceedling 1.2.2, it runs again with the project’s own project file and mixins, which may select another installation through :project ↳ :which_ceedling. The version decides which of Ceedling’s features the extension uses, such as running a test file by its path from Ceedling 1.2.0.
  2. ceedling dumpconfig resolves the project’s configuration, with its mixins and plugin defaults applied.
  3. ceedling files:test lists the project’s test files. The extension then reads each one to find its test functions and parametrized cases.

The extension applies a mixin of its own to every command that reads or runs the project. It enables the report_tests_log_factory plugin’s cppunit report, which is where the extension reads test results. No plugin setup is needed in project.yml. Configuration explains how it combines with your own mixins.

docs.title: Keeping the test list current
docs.text:
The Testing view keeps itself current as the project changes.

  • Editing a test file updates its tests as you type, even before you save.
  • Adding or removing a test file rediscovers the project.
  • Changing project.yml, a mixin file, or the Ceedling in vendor/ceedling rediscovers it too.
  • Changing a setting that affects discovery, such as ceedlingExplorer.projects, rediscovers every project in the folder.

The Testing view’s refresh button rediscovers on demand, for example after upgrading the installed Ceedling gem.

docs.title: Migrating from Ceedling Test Explorer
docs.text:
This extension continues the original Ceedling Test Explorer extension, and most of its settings carry over unchanged.

  • The tests appear in VS Code’s own Testing view, not the third-party Test Explorer view. The Test Explorer UI extension is no longer needed.
  • The ceedlingExplorer.debugConfiguration setting no longer exists. Name each project’s launch configuration in ceedlingExplorer.projects[].debugLaunchConfig instead.
  • launch.json configurations using ${command:ceedlingExplorer.debugTestExecutable} work unchanged.

The Breaking Changes document describes the changes that need action when upgrading.

docs.title: Problem Matching
docs.text: Problem matching reports compiler and linker problems in the editor and the Problems panel. It scans Ceedling’s output for known error, warning, and info lines, much as the problemMatcher of VS Code’s Tasks does. This page covers the setting’s two fields and every property of a custom pattern. The compiler problems guide has patterns for common compilers and linkers.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Problem matching is off by default. The ceedlingExplorer.problemMatching setting turns it on, and the gcc preset suits most projects.

"ceedlingExplorer.problemMatching": {
    "mode": "gcc"
}

Ceedling shows a compiler’s or linker’s output only when that tool fails, so problems appear from failed builds. A file that compiles with only warnings shows none, at Ceedling’s default verbosity. Every build that finishes scans its output, and a cancelled build scans none. A test file’s build replaces the problems its last build reported, and a project’s build replaces those of every build in the project. A fixed problem therefore clears with the next build of the test file or project that reported it. Setting mode to "disabled" clears every problem at once.

docs.title: The setting’s fields
docs.text:
Two fields select the patterns used.

Field Description mode "disabled", the "gcc" preset, or "patterns" for the custom patterns below. By default it is "disabled". patterns Custom pattern objects. With mode set to "patterns", each one scans Ceedling’s output line by line. By default it is [].

docs.title: Pattern properties
docs.text:
Each custom pattern is a regular expression, plus the indexes of its capture groups. A match reports one problem, at the file and lines its groups capture.

Property Description regexp The regular expression matching a problem line, in ECMAScript (JavaScript) syntax. In JSON, each backslash is doubled. regex101 helps while experimenting. Required. message The capture group holding the problem’s message. Required. file The capture group holding the problem’s file. Required. line The capture group holding the problem’s (first) line. Unused when null or absent. lastLine The capture group holding the problem’s last line. Unused when null or absent. column The capture group holding the problem’s (first) column. Unused when null or absent. lastColumn The capture group holding the problem’s last column. Unused when null or absent. severity The severity of the problems this pattern finds: "error", "warning", or "info". By default it is "info". filePrefix Prepended to a relative file path to make it absolute. ${projectPath} becomes the project’s directory. An empty string, the default, means reported paths are already absolute. scanStderr Scan Ceedling’s stderr for problems. Compilers write their diagnostics there. By default it is true. scanStdout Scan Ceedling’s stdout for problems. By default it is false.

This pattern matches GCC’s compiler warnings.

{
    "severity": "warning",
    "filePrefix": "${projectPath}",
    "regexp": "^(.*):(\\d+):(\\d+):\\s+warning:\\s+(.*)$",
    "message": 4,
    "file": 1,
    "line": 2,
    "column": 3
}

A pattern whose regular expression is invalid matches nothing, and the extension’s log warns about it. A pattern missing its regexp, message, or file is skipped, and only the log’s debug level mentions it.

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text: Tests run from VS Code’s Testing view or from the editor, and their results appear in both. This page covers what each kind of run does in Ceedling, how results are shown, how tests are labeled, and the cleanup commands. Debugging has a page of its own, Debugging.

docs.title: Where to run tests
docs.text:
Every test in the Testing view has run and debug buttons, and so does every test file. The editor’s gutter shows the same buttons beside each test function and parametrized case.

The view groups tests by where they come from. A workspace folder holding several Ceedling projects lists each project, by its name, with its test files beneath it. A folder holding one project lists its test files directly. A workspace with several folders adds an entry per folder, labeled Ceedling (folder).

A run of a test file runs it through Ceedling’s test: task. A run of a whole project runs test:all. A run covering several projects runs them one after another. Separate runs of projects in different directories may overlap. Commands within one project directory, or in projects sharing a build directory, never overlap, since Ceedling’s builds there would collide.

docs.title: A single test
docs.text:
Running a single test function runs only that function, through Ceedling’s --test-case filter. Ceedling still compiles the function’s whole test file.

Ceedling’s filter matches by substring, so a filter for test_Add also matches test_AddOverflow. When the filter matches another test in the file, the extension runs the whole file instead, and reports every test in it. The extension’s log says when that happens.

docs.title: Parametrized test cases
docs.text:
Each case of a parametrized test appears beneath its function in the Testing view, as Ceedling runs it. Unity’s TEST_CASE(), TEST_RANGE(), and TEST_MATRIX() all produce cases.

Parametrized tests need one project setting. Unity’s markers take effect only with :unity ↳ :use_param_tests set to true. The Testing view lists each case separately only then.

:unity:
  :use_param_tests: true

Ceedling 1.0.0 also needs test-file preprocessing off, since its preprocessing loses the markers. Set :project ↳ :use_test_preprocessor to :none, its default, or to :mocks. Ceedling 1.1.0 and later handle parametrized tests either way.

Running one case runs all the cases of its function, since Ceedling selects tests by function. Every case reports its own result.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A run reports each test’s outcome in the Testing view once Ceedling finishes the command that ran it. A failed test shows its message at its failing line, in the Testing view and inline in the editor.

A build that fails marks each of its tests errored, with the build’s error. The Test Results panel holds Ceedling’s full output for each run, with every compiler and linker error. Problem matching can also report those errors in the editor and the Problems panel.

A test that crashes is reported as a failure too, through Ceedling’s :use_backtrace setting. Debugging explains its choices.

docs.title: Test labels
docs.text:
The Testing view shortens test and file labels by default, so long names stay readable. Two settings control it, ceedlingExplorer.prettyTestLabel and ceedlingExplorer.prettyTestFileLabel.

A test’s label drops its prefix. For example, test_BlinkTaskShouldToggleLed becomes BlinkTaskShouldToggleLed.

Off On

A test file’s label drops its path, prefix, and extension. For example, test/LEDs/test_BlinkTask.c becomes BlinkTask.

Off On

The prefixes come from the project’s own configuration, :test_runner ↳ :test_prefix and :project ↳ :test_file_prefix.

docs.title: Clean and Clobber
docs.text: The Testing view’s toolbar has Clean and Clobber buttons. They run ceedling clean and ceedling clobber in every Ceedling project in the workspace. Each project’s command waits for any Ceedling build under way in that project to finish. Configuration lists their command IDs, for keyboard shortcuts.

docs.title: After upgrading Ceedling
docs.text: Ceedling 1.2.2 builds each test in a new place, and an earlier release’s build output stays until a clobber. After an upgrade from Ceedling 1.2.0 or 1.2.1, the first build offers to clobber the project. Accepting it clobbers once the runs under way finish. After an upgrade from an earlier release, clobber once with the toolbar button. The Known Issues list the cases where no offer appears.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Most problems show up as a notification, and the extension’s log says more. This page matches each common symptom and message to its cause and fix. When nothing here fits, check the Known Issues before filing a bug report.

docs.title: Reading the log
docs.text:
The extension logs each problem it finds to the Ceedling Explorer output channel. Open the Output panel and choose Ceedling Explorer from its list.

The log shows information, warnings, and errors by default. Raise the channel’s level to Debug to also see every Ceedling command the extension runs, with its working directory and shell. Use the Output panel’s gear menu, or the Developer: Set Log Level… command. A bug report with a debug-level log is far easier to act on.

docs.title: No tests appear
docs.text:
A project that can’t be discovered leaves its whole workspace folder without tests until the problem is fixed. A notification names the problem. Each message below is the start of one.

  • “Could not run 'ceedling version' for project …” Ceedling isn’t installed, or isn’t on the PATH of the shell the extension uses. Check that ceedling version works in a terminal. Set ceedlingExplorer.shellPath to the shell where it does, or ceedlingExplorer.ceedlingCommand to the command that runs it.
  • “Ceedling version … is not supported.” The project runs a Ceedling older than 1.0.0. Upgrade Ceedling, or the copy in the project’s vendor/ceedling.
  • “Ceedling stopped reporting its version for project …” Ceedling itself stopped with an error, which the message quotes. A project file, a mixin, or a :project ↳ :which_ceedling that names a missing installation usually causes it.
  • “Failed to resolve Ceedling's configuration for project …” ceedling dumpconfig failed, and the message quotes Ceedling’s error. Check that the paths in ceedlingExplorer.projects and every mixin exist.
  • “Failed to list the test files of Ceedling project …” ceedling files:test failed. Check the project’s :paths: ↳ :test: entries.
  • “The project path … does not exist or is not a directory.” A ceedlingExplorer.projects[].path names nothing. Paths are relative to the workspace folder.
  • “Both project.yml and ceedling.yml exist in …” Ceedling can’t tell which file is the project. Remove or rename one, or name the one to use in ceedlingExplorer.projects[].path.
  • “ceedlingExplorer.… must be …” A setting holds the wrong kind of value, e.g. a single string where a list belongs. Fix it in settings.json.
  • “The required Ceedling plugin 'report_tests_log_factory' did not take effect …” A configured mixin is invalid, so the extension’s own mixin didn’t apply. Check ceedlingExplorer.mixins and each projects[].mixins.
  • “Failed to load Ceedling project: …” Discovery failed unexpectedly. Please report it, with the log’s copy of the message.

A project the extension can’t find shows no notification at all. That happens when the project file isn’t at the workspace folder’s root, or when a ceedlingExplorer.projects[].path names a directory or YAML file without a project file to go with it. Name the project’s path in ceedlingExplorer.projects.

docs.title: A run shows no results
docs.text:
A build that fails marks each of its tests errored, with the build’s error. The Test Results panel shows Ceedling’s output, with the compiler or linker error in full. Problem matching can also put those errors in the editor.

A test marked errored with “Ceedling reported no result for this test” ran in a build that reported others. Usually the test list is stale. Refresh the Testing view. The log then shows “Ceedling reported results matching no discovered test” for any results the extension couldn’t place.

docs.title: Debugging doesn’t start
docs.text:
Each debugging message names what to fix.

  • “Start debugging from a test’s debug icon in the Testing view …” The configuration was started with F5 or from the Run and Debug view. Only a test’s debug button supplies the test executable. See Debugging.
  • “No debug configuration named '…' found in launch.json.” The project’s debugLaunchConfig doesn’t match any configuration’s "name". A project that names none needs a configuration named ceedling.
  • “The debugger could not be started with '…'.” VS Code rejected the configuration. Check that its type names an installed debugger extension, and that its debugger’s path exists.

docs.title: Coverage shows nothing
docs.text: A coverage run that shows no coverage says why. Each reason is notified once a session, and every run logs it and notes it in the Test Results panel. Code Coverage lists each reason and its fix.

docs.title: After a Ceedling upgrade
docs.text:
Upgrading the installed Ceedling gem needs a refresh of the Testing view, so the extension checks the version again. A change to a project’s vendor/ceedling refreshes it by itself.

From Ceedling 1.2.2, each test builds in a new place. After an upgrade from 1.2.0 or 1.2.1, the extension offers to clobber the project’s old build output. After an upgrade from an earlier release, clobber once with the Testing view’s Clobber button.

A log warning that a project “runs Ceedling … from another installation” means its launcher can’t tell the other installation’s release. Launchers before 1.2.2 can’t (Ceedling#1365). Everything still works, though discovery waits for runs to finish. Upgrading the installed Ceedling to 1.2.2 or later removes the warning.

docs.title: Clean or Clobber fails
docs.text: A notification that “Ceedling clean failed” or “Ceedling clobber failed” means the command failed in at least one project. Run the same command, ceedling clean or ceedling clobber, in a terminal in the project’s directory to see Ceedling’s error.

docs.title: Known issues and bug reports
docs.text: Open problems are listed by Ceedling version in the Known Issues. If yours isn’t there, please file a bug report, with the extension’s version, your Ceedling version, and a debug-level log.
